title: The most valuable step in writing with AI isn't the prompt — it's compounding your revision feedback
dek: Katie took AI from professional coach all the way to writing plugin: first load the model with context, then store every revision note back into the system and let it compound. For her, AI's value isn't just output — it's a support system that steadies her and gets her past the execution wall.
why: Not another prompt demo, but a rare record of how a writer grows her own AI workflow: how to build the context files, how to choose reviewers, even how a non-technical person avoids the pitfalls — concrete enough to copy.
who: Reporters and editors doing content, WeChat public accounts or long-form pieces, plus indie developers building AI into a personal productivity system; especially for anyone stuck with homogenised AI output who wants to build their own workflow.
skip: The trailer before 1:04 and the sponsor read at 21:48 are skippable; the main content is worth it from 8:26 all the way to the end.

points.h: Hiring AI as a coach is about being questioned, not being thought for
points.body: After being laid off while working as an editor and ghostwriter at a crypto company, Katie tried agency-side, client-side and freelancing, and still felt she had hit the end of her own ideas. A real career coach was too expensive — she estimated about $150/hour — so she switched to ChatGPT at $20/month. She wasn't looking for someone to think for her, but for an object to externalise her thinking onto: state her situation, let it question and push back, and especially pull her out of herself when she tends toward catastrophising. She later called this her ‘thinking tool’. She even used it to decide whether to accept Every's column invitation — at the time ChatGPT suggested she try it first, and she has been on that path ever since.

points.h: One person shipping five channels runs on context, not typing speed
points.body: In early 2025, freelancing, Katie badly overcommitted: 8 blog posts, 3 ebooks, 24 LinkedIn posts, 24 X posts and 16 Instagram posts inside a two-week deadline. Getting it done wasn't about writing fast — it was what she only later realised was called context engineering: first write out the company's brand information, product details, audience and differentiation point by point, then let the model generate. Building that context up front was laborious, but once the foundation was in place, production speed afterwards became very fast. She admits she repeated the same overcommitment six months later — the method never cured her overcommitting.

points.h: Without underlying information, style constraints just spin in place
points.body: On what to put into a project first, Katie is clear: not rules like ‘use these words, avoid those’ or ‘keep the reading level low’, but first a base dossier on who the reader is, where it hurts, how the product maps to that pain, who the competitors are and what the differentiation is. She says this was her instinct from writing style guides in content marketing — only now she feeds it to AI. Once the foundational material is in place, only then do tone, wording and syntax constraints come in. Her position on ‘style’: wording questions will be argued over forever, but without underlying information, style constraints just spin in place.

points.h: The model is the kitchen; fresh ingredients can only be brought in by a human
points.body: The ‘data’ she means isn't general background, but first-hand material from after the model's knowledge cutoff, or that only exists in the real physical world: research the company did itself, third-party reports, specific personal experience. If you just let the model write a ‘style guide’ from what it already knows, the output is commoditized information. So what she needs a human for is the ‘last mile’: bringing new material the model doesn't have into the system. Her metaphor is that the model is the kitchen and the process is chopping and cooking, but the fresh ingredients must be carried into the kitchen by a person — the quality and freshness of the input ultimately decide whether a piece is worth reading.

points.h: AI as supportive technology is as strong as AI as production tool
points.body: Katie talks about a layer rarely said in public: she has bipolar disorder, experiences high-energy periods, and also faces very long, very long lows. For her, AI's value isn't just ‘high output’ — it's lowering the friction of daily life, making it easier for her to function as a person who can keep going. She put off booking a family doctor for three years, and eventually had Codex automatically find nearby doctors who take her insurance and accept new patients and book one; her inbox is also handed to automation to filter out the mail that genuinely needs her reply, rather than her digging through a pile of subscription notifications every day looking for a ‘bomb’. In her own words: AI as supportive technology is as powerful as productive technology.

points.h: A career coach isn't one prompt, it's a project
points.body: That simple ‘be my career coach’ prompt has now become a standalone project in Codex: her own profile and role positioning, Every's brand positioning intelligence, article performance data exported from the CMS, a validation folder dedicated to collecting reader praise, and Q2/Q3 OKRs. Much of the material she didn't organise by hand: she learned Alex Duffy's method of having AI interview her, drawing the thoughts out of her head and turning them into documents. She now increasingly talks to it directly by voice, ‘thinking out loud’, having it prioritise, do project management, maintain the kanban. She has even forgotten what's on the kanban, and only asks for the deadline of a given deliverable when she needs it.

points.h: Writing should be like engineering: correct the same problem only once
points.body: Compound Writing started by forking Kieran's Compound Engineering: in engineering, the system should remember every piece of feedback, correct the same problem only once, and do it right automatically next time; writing should be the same. She mapped the engineering version's brainstorming, planning, working and reviewing onto writing's brainstorm, outline, draft and review, and designed three kinds of review: a substantive edit for overall structure and argument, a line edit for sentence-by-sentence polish, and finally a publication-ready pass. She no longer opens a web chat window, but runs this system in the Claude or ChatGPT desktop app, with the style guide, sample articles and other context inside, so the human only needs to bring in fresh information. At the time of recording the plugin was already downloadable from Every's GitHub.

points.h: This plugin is a gym, not a ghostwriting machine
points.body: She calls the plugin a gym; the goal is to make the user stronger, not to let AI ghostwrite. She breaks the authors she loves into invokable reviewer skills: Vonnegut on ‘start as close to the end as possible, every sentence must earn its place, give the reader a character to root for’; Hitchcock on the ‘bomb under the table’ — if you let the audience see the countdown first, one second of shock becomes five minutes of suspense. She builds these frameworks straight into the editing step, so after writing you can invoke Vonnegut, Hitchcock, Sorkin, Sedaris to look at your draft. She thinks non-professional writers may benefit even more, because there's no stock attachment of ‘how I used to write it better’ in the way.

terms.def: Having AI remember every piece of feedback, give the same correction only once, then apply it automatically so output keeps improving.
Katie's plugin that ports Compound Engineering into the writing process, compounding style, structure and review feedback.
Loading brand, audience, competitor and other background information into the system before letting the model write, setting boundaries for the AI.
AI that doesn't produce content but lowers the friction of life and execution, making it easier to get done what needs doing.
A general interface standard connecting models to external data and apps; Katie uses it to link small apps with the tools she uses.

quotes.text: Clarity, it turns out, doesn't arrive gift wrapped from a digital assistant or even a human coach. It's something I had to dig out for myself, question by question and prompt by prompt.
But when you have that environment set up, you can just kind of run and like run fast.

So the data is the unique insight, the data point that the model doesn't have access to yet, the personal experience, all of those things that are working are ultimately going to make the writing unique.
AI is just as powerful as a supportive technology.
So compounding is the idea that every piece of feedback that you give to AI should feed back into the system to improve the next output.

if there's a bomb under the table and it explodes, that's a one moment of surprise. But if you have people sitting around the table and you show the audience the bomb under the table and say this bomb will go off in five minutes, now you have five minutes of suspense.
what I want to challenge the AI community with is thinking about how we can expand those kinds of opportunities to more people and more kinds of people in more different places.
